item.text:
Based solely on the supplied text, the following are potential loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting defects—not assurances that particular operations would be lawful. **Section 2(1)(B)’s risk-based catchall could close several apparent exclusions, and an exemption from this bill would not itself authorize conduct prohibited by other laws or license conditions.** A definitive assessment would require reviewing those authorities as well.

### Definitions and scope

1. **§ 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel rather than aggregate threshold.** The 10,000-metric-ton threshold applies to a “single vessel,” with no aggregation across vessels, affiliated operators, or a common project. A fleet could collectively recover substantially more while each vessel remains outside subparagraph (A), subject to the catchall in subparagraph (B).

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Exact threshold boundaries.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year, or recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower, falls outside subparagraph (A). Neither boundary limits the catchall in subparagraph (B).

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual measurement period.** “Per year” could mean a calendar year, a rolling 12-month period, or an operating year. The choice affects both threshold compliance and the treatment of operations spanning year-end.

4. **§§ 2(1)(A), 5(a)—Unclear threshold-trigger date.** The text does not say whether an operation becomes prohibited only upon exceeding 10,000 tons, or whether exceeding that amount makes earlier recovery during the same year unlawful. That uncertainty directly affects the number of daily penalties.

5. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined recovery and weight accounting.** “Recovery” does not identify whether material is counted when disturbed, collected, lifted aboard, or landed, and the bill supplies no wet-weight, dry-weight, or mineral-content standard. Those choices could materially change whether an operation crosses the threshold.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Attributing recovery to a vessel.** The text does not allocate recovery among seabed collectors, lift vessels, support vessels, and receiving vessels. Operations using multiple vessels or non-vessel installations therefore present a coverage question, although subparagraph (B) could reach them.

7. **§ 2(1)(A)—Depth measurement.** The bill does not specify a depth datum or how to treat recovery along a site that crosses the 200-meter boundary. It also does not expressly explain how mixed-depth recovery counts toward the annual threshold.

8. **§ 2(1)—“Commercial” does not require commercial purpose.** Despite its label, the definition contains no requirement of sale, profit, or commercial intent. Scientific or demonstration recovery could therefore qualify, while small commercial operations could fall outside subparagraph (A).

9. **§ 2(1)(A)—Broad mineral-resource coverage.** “Other mineral resources” is undefined and extends beyond polymetallic nodules. This creates uncertainty over coverage of other seabed extraction, including operations not ordinarily described as deep-seabed mining.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—Undefined “Secretary.”** The bill never identifies the official empowered to make comparable-risk determinations. Section 6 expressly names the Secretary of State, and section 4 names NOAA, but neither clearly assigns this authority.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—Unspecified risk-comparison standard.** The provision identifies no risk metrics, reference operation, probability threshold, or method for comparing different ecosystems and extraction technologies. Because subparagraph (A) covers operations of widely varying scale, even the comparator is uncertain.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure or timing.** The bill does not specify whether determinations apply to individual projects or entire activity classes, or when they become operative. Generally applicable administrative-law requirements may supply safeguards, but the text leaves important notice and implementation questions unresolved.

13. **§ 2(1)(B)—Catchall potentially reaches non-mining conduct.** “Any activity” is not expressly confined to mineral recovery, commercial activity, vessels, or depths greater than 200 meters. Its breadth creates scope and fair-notice concerns, particularly when paired with criminal penalties.

14. **§ 2(2)—Incomplete entity coverage.** “U.S. person” includes citizens and state-organized corporations but does not expressly include LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, or entities organized solely under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. To the extent those entities are not corporations organized under the laws of a “State,” their conduct abroad may fall outside section 3(a)’s nationality-based reach.

15. **§ 2(2)—Residents and foreign subsidiaries.** The definition omits noncitizen U.S. residents and foreign-incorporated companies, including U.S.-owned subsidiaries. Their overseas conduct is not expressly covered merely because of U.S. residence or ownership, although participating U.S. citizens and domestic conduct may remain exposed.

16. **§ 3(a)—Geographic reach is undefined.** “In the United States” is not defined to address territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. Those distinctions matter particularly for foreign persons whom the nationality-based prohibition does not reach.

17. **§ 3(a)—Participation and supporting activities.** “Engage in” is undefined, and the bill does not expressly address financing, directing, contracting for, processing, transporting, or buying minerals from prohibited recovery. Some participation may be covered through ordinary liability doctrines, but the text does not establish a comprehensive supply-chain prohibition.

### Exceptions

18. **§ 3(b)—Exploration-license exception may shelter substantial recovery.** The exception covers “mining conducted under an exploration license” without its own volume ceiling or restriction to noncommercial recovery. Its practical scope depends on what the underlying license lawfully permits; the exception does not expand that license.

19. **§ 3(b)—Unspecified licensing authority.** The text does not identify a qualifying licensing statute, issuing country, or international authority. That leaves uncertainty over whether foreign or international exploration licenses qualify alongside U.S. licenses.

20. **§ 3(b)—Grandfathering attaches to licenses, not existing operations.** A license need only have been issued before enactment; mining need not already have begun. Accordingly, previously licensed but inactive projects could claim the exception.

21. **§ 3(b)—Renewals, amendments, and transfers.** The bill does not explain whether a grandfathered license retains its status after renewal, extension, assignment, or material amendment. It also supplies no independent limits on expanded acreage, vessels, or recovery under such a license.

22. **§ 3(b)—No express validity or compliance condition.** The exception does not expressly require a license to remain valid and in good standing or the mining to comply with its terms. “Conducted under” may imply those requirements, but clearer language would reduce disputes over expired, suspended, or breached licenses.

23. **§ 3(c)—Environmental-assessment purpose is undefined.** The exception has no requirement that assessment be the sole or primary purpose and no rule for mixed assessment and commercial activities. A genuine assessment purpose could therefore support an exemption claim even where mineral recovery also has commercial value.

24. **§ 3(c)—No approval requirement or operational limits.** The exception requires no designated agency approval, independent research protocol, recovery cap, duration limit, or restriction on selling recovered material. The text consequently provides few express safeguards against oversized or commercially oriented assessment projects.

### Registry and reporting

25. **§§ 2(3), 4(a)—Registry coverage does not track prohibited activity.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less are excluded from registration even if they conduct prohibited recovery. Conversely, large recovery-equipped vessels must register even when their operations are below the mining threshold or exempt.

26. **§ 2(3)—Unspecified tonnage and equipment standards.** “Gross tons” does not identify the applicable vessel-measurement convention, and “equipped for” does not distinguish installed, temporary, modular, or inactive equipment. These omissions can create disputes over registry eligibility.

27. **§ 4(a)—No geographic or nationality limit.** Read literally, “each covered vessel” includes foreign vessels operating wholly abroad. The absence of a jurisdictional nexus creates uncertainty over the intended reach and practical enforceability of registration.

28. **§ 4—Undefined operator and registration timing.** The text does not allocate responsibility among owners, charterers, managers, and contractors, or set a registration deadline. “Registered operator” in subsection (b) also differs from subsection (a)’s instruction to register the vessel.

29. **§ 4(b)—Reporting duty arguably depends on prior registration.** Reports are required from “[e]ach registered operator,” rather than every operator required to register. An operator that fails to register could argue that the separate reporting duty never attached, although the registration violation would remain.

30. **§ 4(b)—Insufficient reporting specifications.** The bill supplies no quarterly submission deadlines or required data fields for tonnage, depth, location, license status, or claimed exceptions. Operator certification alone does not establish a verification, record-retention, or independent-audit system.

31. **§§ 4–5—No express registry penalties.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. Other generally applicable laws may address some misconduct, including certain false statements, but the bill supplies no specific penalty for simple registry noncompliance.

### Enforcement and timing

32. **§ 5—Incomplete enforcement machinery.** The bill does not designate a civil enforcement authority or specify assessment procedures, collection mechanisms, inspection authority, or administrative subpoenas. Existing authority may fill some gaps, but NOAA’s receipt of reports does not itself resolve them.

33. **§ 5(a)—Unclear unit of civil violation.** The penalty is capped for “each day on which the violation occurs,” without stating whether simultaneous vessels, projects, or prohibited acts generate separate daily violations. This could substantially change maximum exposure.

34. **§§ 5(a), 8—Enactment versus effective-date conflict.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness by 180 days. The stronger harmonized reading may be that section 3 cannot be violated before it takes effect, but the conflicting language invites disputes over attempted earlier liability.

35. **§§ 2(1)(B), 5(b)—Criminal notice and willfulness questions.** Criminal liability depends on a willful violation, but the bill leaves unclear how an operator receives notice of a comparable-risk determination and what knowledge that prosecution requires. The undefined decisionmaker and risk standard compound this issue; they do not automatically invalidate the criminal provision.

### International agreement and duration

36. **§ 6—Unclear negotiating deadline and limited required outcome.** “Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly distinguish a deadline to initiate efforts from one to complete negotiations. It requires seeking an agreement, not securing one, and provides no fallback if negotiations fail.

37. **§ 6—No automatic international implementation.** Seeking an agreement does not itself bind foreign operators or implement resulting obligations domestically. “Prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3” also leaves unclear whether equivalence includes that section’s broad exceptions.

38. **§ 7(a)—No commissioned report or substantive decision standard.** The bill neither directs nor funds a National Academies report, sets a delivery deadline, nor defines “serious harm.” It also leaves unclear whether the congressional finding concerns all commercial deep-seabed mining or particular technologies, locations, or conditions.

39. **§ 7(a)—Only the prohibition ends upon a congressional finding.** A qualifying joint resolution ends section 3’s prohibition, but does not expressly terminate registration, reporting, or other provisions. That may be intentional, but the resulting post-prohibition regulatory regime is not explained.

40. **§§ 7(a)–(b), 8—Unconditional sunset overrides the safety-based duration.** The entire Act expires ten years after enactment even without a report or congressional no-serious-harm finding. Because effectiveness is delayed 180 days, the operative prohibition lasts less than ten years absent earlier termination.

41. **§ 7(b)—No express savings or transition clause.** The sunset does not explain the treatment of outstanding reports, pending proceedings, or accrued liabilities. The general federal savings statute may preserve penalties and liabilities, so sunset should not be assumed to erase prior violations.
